name: Patched
describes: White finishes that have been mended: plaster cut back and made good, cracks filled, fibrous panels re-tied, broken parts of casts rejoined, soiled casts repainted, limewash renewed. A repair reads because it differs from the old surface in suction, texture, whiteness and soiling age, and because its edge is a line.

limePatch.state: Loose plaster is cut back to a sound face with a slight undercut, and the patch is built in thin coats of a mix matched to the original (aggregate grading, proportions, hair, gypsum), keyed and kept from drying too fast.
limePatch.source: Napier, W. & Jenkins, M. (2018) Inform Guide: Plain Lime Plastering. Historic Environment Scotland, https://www.historicenvironment.scot/archives-and-research/publications/publication/?publicationId=67d4d72c-7b8c-4622-a244-a94b01090177

fineFills.state: Fine cracks, small holes and minor imperfections are filled with proprietary filler mixed with crushed chalk (whiting) and sanded flush.

suctionMismatch.state: A repair gauged with gypsum sets with less shrinkage but differs in suction, which changes how limewash or distemper looks over it: the patch shows through the decoration.

castRepairs.state: Slender attachments of fresh casts drop off and are replaced; old casts carry historic repairs, dents and hairline cracks, which conservators now leave where stable.
castRepairs.source: Brigham, W.T. (1874), pp. 27-29, as quoted in Payne, E.M. (2020) The Conservation of Plaster Casts in the Nineteenth Century. Studies in Conservation 65(1), 37-58, https://doi.org/10.1080/00393630.2019.1610845; Puisto, J. (2014) David revealed. V&A Blog, https://www.vam.ac.uk/blog/caring-for-our-collections/david-revealed

castRepainting.state: Casts grimed by neglect were cleaned and given a further 'refreshing' layer of paint; the coating stack stays thin.

coatingStackThickness.asReported: approximately 40 um to 280 um, no more than four layers

fibrousRepair.state: Failed plaster is cleaned off and ties re-wadded; weak areas are backed with a reinforcing layer of hessian stuck on with casting plaster; for extensive damage, glass-reinforced gypsum is substituted.
fibrousRepair.source: Harrison, D. (1999) Dramatic Plasterwork: Fibrous Plaster in Theatres. The Building Conservation Directory, https://www.buildingconservation.com/articles/theatre/theatre.htm

limewashRenewal.state: Limewash is renewed rather than patched: a fresh campaign of coats over the whole face, externally about every five years.

bySubstance.lime-plaster: A patch of a metre or less with a slightly undercut, sometimes visible edge; a different trowel texture and a cleaner white than its soiled surround until it too soils.
bySubstance.fibrous-plaster: Repairs mostly behind the face (new wads, backing hessian); on the face, a filled joint or a replaced length whose whiteness differs.
bySubstance.plaster-of-paris: Rejoined fingers, noses and attributes with a fine join line; fills that are smoother or whiter than the cast; paint layers that blur fine detail.
bySubstance.limewash: No patches: whole faces renewed in campaigns, each leaving a thin layer.

drivers.driver: piece age and seed (where and when a repair happened)
arris proximity (knocks and losses at edges and projections)
soiling age of the surround versus the patch

unverified.reason: No sourced distribution of patch sizes; 'a metre or less' is a description, not a measurement.
No measured colour difference between patch and original was found.
Fills reading smoother or whiter is the expected trace; not measured in the sources read.

sources: Harrison, D. (1999) Dramatic Plasterwork: Fibrous Plaster in Theatres. The Building Conservation Directory.
Napier, W. & Jenkins, M. (2018) Inform Guide: Plain Lime Plastering. Historic Environment Scotland.
Payne, E.M. (2020) Studies in Conservation 65(1), 37-58, https://doi.org/10.1080/00393630.2019.1610845 (quoting Brigham 1874)
Puisto, J. (2014) David revealed. V&A Blog.
